extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, and others researching patent claim scope and estoppel across jurisdictions
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the legal doctrine of prosecution history (file-wrapper) estoppel and how various jurisdictions treat prosecution history in claim construction and the doctrine of equivalents, including key U.S. case law (Festo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: prosecution history estoppel (file-wrapper estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine indicating that a person who filed a patent application and then makes narrowing amendments to the application to accommodate the patent law may be precluded from invoking the doctrine of equivalents to broaden the scope of their claims to cover subject matter ceded by the amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the basic effect: narrowing amendments during prosecution can limit a patentee's ability to assert equivalents for the amended elements. Although primarily a U.S. term, the issue of using prosecution history in claim construction arises in other jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canada: admissibility and rejection of file-wrapper estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents in Canada are subject to purposive construction; extrinsic evidence is not permitted, and Canadian courts emphatically reject 'file wrapper estoppel'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of Dec 13, 2018, new section 53.1 of the Patent Act makes prosecution history evidence admissible before the Court for the purposes of claim construction. Nevertheless, Canadian jurisprudence generally bars use of negotiations with the Patent Office to establish equivalents or to determine claim scope; no distinction is drawn between literal and substantive infringement when excluding file-wrapper evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Germany: general exclusion with limited later nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: The German Federal Court of Justice ruled (2002) that 'issues derived from prosecution history cannot be taken into account in the assessment of the scope of protection of a patent, even with regard to the requirement of legal certainty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A later 14 June 2016 BGH ruling indicated that statements made during prosecution may indicate how the skilled person construes a patent, but such indications 'must not readily be relied on as the sole basis of claim construction' — i.e., limited, non-decisive use is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ireland: inadmissibility of patentee's file views
rubrics_metrics.description: The Irish Supreme Court has ruled that 'evidence from the file which reflects the views of the patentee as to the construction of the claims is inadmissible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court practice excludes patentee's own prosecution statements from being used to construe claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Netherlands: permissive use of examination file
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dutch Supreme Court has held that when a third party invokes the examination file to confirm an interpretation they defend, public data from the examination file may be involved in patent interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court found that the reasonable doubt threshold does not restrict involving public examination-file data in construing the patent; the Dutch approach is effectively more permissive than many other European jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Kingdom: general discouragement, narrow exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: UK courts have ruled that use of the examination file in aiding construction of a patent should be discouraged except where the file includes 'objective information about and commentary on experiments'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner-file material is generally discouraged as an aid to claim construction in the UK, with limited admissibility when it provides objective factual experimental information.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Federal Circuit (pre-Supreme Court Festo): complete-bar rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (Nov 2000) set a complete bar rule: a narrowing amendment that is related to statutory requirements for a patent will completely bar the patentee from asserting the doctrine of equivalents for the amended claim element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit stated: (1) an amendment that narrows the scope of a claim for any reason related to statutory requirements will give rise to a complete bar with respect to the amended claim element; (2) a 'voluntary' claim amendment that narrows the scope for a reason related to statutory requirements will give rise to prosecution history estoppel as to the amended element; and (3) an amendment followed by failure to explain the reasons during prosecution can give rise to estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Supreme Court (Festo): presumptive bar and patentee's rebuttal burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court overturned the Federal Circuit's complete bar, adopting a presumptive bar approach: narrowing amendments may give rise to prosecution history estoppel, but the patentee can rebut the presumption by showing specific circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome the presumptive bar the patentee must establish that: (1) the equivalent was unforeseeable at the time the claim was drafted; (2) the amendment did not surrender the particular equivalent in question; or (3) there was some reason why the patentee could not have recited the equivalent in the claim. The Court emphasized caution in disrupting inventing-community expectations and assigned the burden to patentees to show that the amendment did not surrender particular equivalents.
